headline: Alberta votes on starting to leave Canada.
summary: On Monday, voters in Alberta, Canada's oil province, decide whether to begin the legal process toward a referendum on leaving the country. It is not a vote to leave. Premier Danielle Smith called the vote and wants to stay. A recent poll put support for starting the process at 23%. Separatist leaders say they would be thrilled with 30%.

cover_question.q: Can part of a country just leave?

cover_answer: Not yet. Monday only asks whether to start the process.
table_question: If one room in the house wants to be its own house, who gets a say?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: Canada is made of big pieces called provinces, like rooms in a house. One room, Alberta, has lots of oil, and some people there want it to be its own house. On Monday the grown-ups in Alberta vote on whether to even begin that long process. Most people there want to stay, and nobody moves anywhere this week.
5-7.why: Rooms in a house. A six-year-old can picture one room wanting to leave, and the ending tells them nothing moves.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old takes one vivid feature for the whole event, so the country becomes a house and Alberta a room that wants to be its own house, with the oil as why the room matters. Cantor's finding is that this age fears for its own home, so the script ends with nobody moving this week. Expect "will our house split?" No.

8-12.script: Alberta sells oil and has fought Canada's government over oil rules and a carbon tax. Separatist parties used to get 1% or 2% of the vote. Then came pandemic rules and the 2022 trucker convoy, and the anger found a new cause. Leaving is a long checklist. Monday is only the first box.
8-12.why: Oil, tax, pandemic, convoy, vote. A chain with a checklist at the end.
8-12.why_long: Eight-to-twelve-year-olds are working out chains of cause and effect, so the script hands them one: oil, a carbon tax, pandemic rules, the convoy, a vote. The checklist is the mechanism, and the first box is all Monday decides. Expect "what if yes wins?" The legal process toward a real referendum starts, and the premier wants to stay.

13-17.script: Why hold a vote you hope loses? Alberta's premier called Monday's, wants to stay, and calls 23% support "too high for my liking." Second: separatists met State Department officials three times. A former premier calls it "bonkers." Should a region pitch itself abroad before its people vote?
13-17.why: A vote she hopes loses, and a movement that went to Washington first.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things: a premier called a vote she wants to lose, and she calls 23% too high. The script adds a movement that went to Washington before its own voters and asks if that is fair play. Let them take the separatists' side first. Expect "would the US take Alberta?" State says only that the vote is Alberta's.

5-7.q: Can part of a country just leave?
5-7.a: Not just like that. It takes votes and years of talking. Monday only asks whether to start, and about one in four say yes.

8-12.q: Why do they want to leave?
8-12.a: Oil. Alberta says Ottawa's climate rules and carbon tax hurt its business.
The legal process toward a real referendum starts. That would take years.

13-17.q: Why is Canada's prime minister popular there?
13-17.a: Carney backs a pipeline to the coast and fights Trump's trade war.
Three meetings with State officials, they say. State says it's Alberta's call.
